extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers outlining novels (authors, plotters, aspiring novelists)
extracted.subtask_description: A how-to guide for plotting a novel using Blake Snyder's Save the Cat! 15-beat framework, including act/scene breakdowns, beat percentage placements, and what should happen in each beat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-act word-count division
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide total word count into three acts: First Act ≈ 25%, Second Act ≈ 50%, Third Act ≈ 25%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for an 80,000-word novel, first act ≈ 20,000; second act ≈ 40,000; third act ≈ 20,000. Use this as a planning blueprint, not a rigid rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene length and scene-count targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a target scene length (recommended ~1,500 words) to divide acts into scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended scenes between 1,000 and 2,000 words (sweet spot ≈ 1,500). Example: 20,000-word act / 1,500 ≈ 14 scenes. Round up if needed; this is a planning tool, not mandatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place beats using percentage locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Locate each of the 15 beats by multiplying total word count or total scene count by the beat's percentage location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can use either words or scenes. Example: Midpoint at 50% → 56 scenes × 0.5 = scene 28; or 80,000 words × 0.5 = 40,000 words. Author prefers using scene counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening Image (0%–1%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single scene beat that shows a 'before' snapshot of the protagonist and the flawed world they live in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This image sets the tone and establishes the protagonist's starting point; it contrasts with the Final Image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme Stated (5%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single scene beat in which someone (not the protagonist) makes a statement that hints at what the protagonist will learn by the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually a line of dialogue or an offhand remark that foreshadows the lesson or theme the hero must learn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup (1%–10%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A multi-scene beat showing the protagonist's life and world (with flaws), introducing important supporting characters and the protagonist's initial goal (what they think will fix their life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish stakes, ordinary world, and the protagonist's mistaken assumption or immediate objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalyst (10%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single scene beat where a life-changing event happens to the protagonist, catapulting them into a new world or way of thinking—after which there's no going back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the inciting incident that forces the story into motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate (10%–20%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A multi-scene beat where the protagonist debates what to do next; shows reluctance to change and internal questions like 'Should I do this?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this section to demonstrate uncertainty and to raise personal stakes before the protagonist commits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break Into Two (20%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single scene beat where the protagonist accepts the call to adventure and leaves their comfort zone—bridging Act 1 and Act 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marks decision point: protagonist moves into new world or new way of thinking; the main story proper begins here.

rubrics_metrics.name: B Story (22%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single scene beat introducing a new character (love interest, mentor, friend, nemesis, family member) who will help the hero learn the story's theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often provides emotional counterpoint and helps the protagonist internalize the theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fun and Games (20%–50%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A multi-scene beat where the reader sees the protagonist either thriving or struggling in the new world—showcasing the premise's promise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the 'promise of the premise' section; show the core pleasures or conflicts of the story world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midpoint (50%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single scene beat where Fun and Games culminates in either a 'false victory' or a 'false defeat'; raises the stakes and forces real change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a kiss or declaration in romance, a game-changing twist in thrillers, or a public crowning moment. Should push protagonist toward real change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad Guys Close In (50%–75%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A multi-scene beat where internal 'bad guys' (fears/false beliefs) and external antagonists close in—either worsening things after a false victory or improving things after a false defeat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Escalate pressure on protagonist; show consequences of earlier choices and deepen conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: All Is Lost (75%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single scene beat where something happens that, combined with the closing-in threat, pushes the protagonist to their lowest point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the apparent annihilation or heartbreak moment—the emotional nadir of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark Night of the Soul (75%–80%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A multi-scene beat where the protagonist processes everything and experiences their darkest hour—right before figuring out the solution and learning the theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sequence internalizes the crisis and sets up the revelation that leads to Break Into Three.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break Into Three (80%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single scene beat where the protagonist realizes what must be done to fix external problems and, more importantly, their internal problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the aha/plan moment, often born from combining knowledge from the B Story with new resolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale (80%–99%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A multi-scene beat where the protagonist proves they have learned the theme and acts on the plan from Break Into Three.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong finale contains five parts (Gathering the Team; Executing the Plan; High Tower Surprise; Dig Deep Down; Execution of New Plan). The author recommends planning roughly 3 scenes for Gathering/Executing/High Tower Surprise and 2 scenes for Dig Deep Down and Execution of New Plan, but this is flexible. Aim for pacing that ramps toward the end—fewer scenes = quicker pace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Image (99%–100%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single scene beat showing an 'after' snapshot of the protagonist's life and how much they've changed since the Opening Image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Should mirror or contrast the Opening Image to reveal the protagonist's growth and the story's thematic resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale — Gathering the Team
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the Finale: protagonist rounds up friends and gathers tools/supplies needed to execute the plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often a short series of scenes to prepare for the climactic action; recommended ~3 scenes in the example scene map.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale — Executing the Plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the Finale: protagonist and crew put the plan into action; may involve sacrifices of secondary characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows tactics and forward motion; recommended ~3 scenes in the example map and can include costs to raise stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale — The High Tower Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the Finale: a twist or surprise forces the protagonist to prove their worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce an unexpected obstacle that tests the protagonist and heightens drama; recommended ~3 scenes in the example map.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale — Dig Deep Down
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the Finale: with no backup plan the protagonist must find inner strength/courage to overcome internal antagonist (fear/false belief).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pivotal internal turning point; recommended ~2 scenes in the example map where the protagonist must access personal growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale — Execution of New Plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the Finale: after overcoming internal barriers, the protagonist takes action against the external antagonist and succeeds (or fails with a clear point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure there is narrative purpose if the protagonist fails; otherwise show the successful application of the lesson/plan; recommended ~2 scenes in the example map.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine structure with character change
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure alone isn't enough—pair the beat framework with a protagonist who needs and undergoes meaningful change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structure as a blueprint for timing and pacing while the character arc supplies emotional stakes; structure + change = a story worth telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing guidance toward the end
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend ramping pacing toward the finale: fewer scenes equal a quicker pace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribute scenes in the Finale to accelerate momentum (example distribution provided); adapt distribution to desired pacing but be intentional about acceleration.
